messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  (none)

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  (none)

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

John, a 57-year-old North American interior designer, was involved in a life-threatening accident about six months ago. The traumatic event occurred while he was driving home from a client meeting on a busy highway. A sudden and violent collision with another vehicle left him disoriented and severely injured. Since then, John's daily life has been fraught with vivid triggers that continually remind him of the harrowing experience. John’s triggers are specific and potent: any imagery of cars being hit by an accident sends waves of fear through his body. Even the sound of car horns or screeching tires can set off a chain reaction of anxiety, plunging him back into the moment of impact. During conversations about accidents at work or among friends, John feels a profound sense of discomfort and unease. John’s occupation as an interior designer has become increasingly challenging due to these triggers. He often avoids projects that involve driving long distances to client sites or attending meetings in high-traffic areas. This avoidance has led to strained relationships with clients who have grown frustrated by his reluctance to visit certain locations. His social life, already affected by his recent divorce, has also suffered as he withdraws from gatherings where the topic of accidents might come up. The accident has deeply shaken John’s sense of self and trust in his own body. He now harbors a pervasive belief that his body is unreliable, unable to protect him or perform basic functions without triggering painful memories. This fear makes it difficult for John to engage fully in physical activities or even simple daily tasks. The trauma has led him to feel like he doesn’t know himself anymore—a sentiment that haunts him as he struggles to reconcile his pre-accident self with the person he is now. John’s negative appraisals are further compounded by a sense of permanent damage. He believes he has been irrevocably altered for the worse, and this belief perpetuates a cycle of doubt and fear in his daily life. His body’s response to triggers only reinforces these beliefs, making it difficult for him to see any possibility of recovery. Despite these challenges, John finally sought help when his avoidance behaviors began to interfere significantly with both his professional and personal life. He is most afraid that he will never feel safe or secure again, but he also holds hope that therapy might help him regain some sense of control over his body and identity. The prospect of reclaiming a semblance of normalcy drives John’s desire for support, even as he grapples with the lingering shadows of the accident.
